lead: Memory must be given to many programs at the same time. Different strategies decide how the main memory is split and how a process sees its own address space. The idea is to use RAM efficiently and to protect processes from each other. These strategies are used in every modern OS, from phones to servers.
prereq: You need: address translation basics from Unit 1.

blocks.text: In fixed partitioning the RAM is divided into blocks of equal size before any process arrives. Each block can hold one process only. The size is chosen by the OS designer.
Fixed partitions are simple to implement. The OS only needs a table of free blocks. They cause internal fragmentation because a process may not use the whole block.
Variable partitioning creates a hole of any size that fits the arriving process. The OS keeps a free‑list of holes. Allocation uses first‑fit, best‑fit or worst‑fit policies.
Variable partitions reduce internal fragmentation but can leave many small holes. This is external fragmentation.

items: Use fixed partitions for embedded systems with predictable workloads.
Use variable partitions when process sizes vary widely.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this "memory allocation strategies".
Paging removes external fragmentation. Memory is divided into equal pages, typically 4 KB or 16 KB. A process address space is also divided into pages of the same size.
The OS keeps a page table. Each entry maps a logical page number to a physical frame number.
Segmentation keeps the logical view of a program. A segment can be code, data or stack. Each segment has a base address and a limit.
Segmentation gives a more natural view but can still suffer external fragmentation. Modern OSes often combine both: each segment is divided into pages.

items: Paging is preferred when fast allocation and deallocation are needed.
Segmentation is useful when programs need separate logical regions.

blocks.text: A logical address (also called virtual address) is generated by the CPU while a program runs.
The OS translates the logical address to a physical address that points to a real byte in RAM.
Translation uses a base register and a limit register in simple schemes.
The base register holds the start of the process region in physical memory. The limit register holds the size of that region.
If the logical address is greater than or equal to the limit, the OS raises an out‑of‑bounds fault.

blocks.where: Physical is the physical address; Base is the value in the base register; Logical is the logical address.

blocks.text: When paging is used, the translation also adds the offset inside the page after looking up the frame number.
Choosing a strategy depends on the workload. Real‑time systems often use fixed partitions for predictability. General‑purpose OSes use paging for flexibility.

examples.question: Physical memory = 64 KB, page size = 16 KB, base register = 0x8000, logical address = 0x2A3F. Compute the physical address using the simple base‑plus‑offset method.
steps: Convert base register to decimal: 0x8000 = 32768 bytes.
Convert logical address to decimal: 0x2A3F = 10815 bytes.
Check that 0xAA3F < 64 KB (65536 bytes). It fits.
examples.check:
base = 0x8000
logical = 0x2A3F
physical = base + logical
print(hex(physical))
print(physical)

traps: Confusing logical address with physical address; the logical value must be added to the base.
Forgetting that the limit register must be checked before translation; otherwise out‑of‑bounds errors are missed.
Using page size in the simple base‑plus‑offset formula; page size is only needed for paging calculations.
Assuming any address fits in memory; always verify that the final physical address is below the total RAM size.

quiz.q: What is the name of the register that holds the start of a process region in physical memory?
Explain why fixed partitions cause internal fragmentation.
quiz.a: Each partition has a fixed size. If a process needs less memory than the partition size, the remaining part cannot be used by other processes, leading to wasted space inside the allocated block.

quiz.q: A system uses 8 KB pages. A process generates the logical address 0x1C23. Find the page number and offset.
quiz.a: Page size = 8 KB = 0x2000. Page number = 0x1C23 // 0x2000 = 0. Offset = 0x1C23 % 0x2000 = 0x1C23 = 7203 decimal.

quiz.q: A workload has many short‑lived processes of similar size. Which memory allocation strategy would minimise fragmentation and why?
quiz.a: Variable partitioning with a best‑fit policy. Short‑lived processes free holes quickly, and best‑fit places each process in the smallest hole that fits, reducing external fragmentation.
External fragmentation is the existence of small free memory blocks scattered throughout RAM that cannot satisfy a larger allocation request.

quiz.q: If a process has base register 0x4000 and limit register 0x2000, what happens when it tries to access logical address 0x2500?
quiz.a: Logical address 0x2500 exceeds the limit 0x2000. The OS raises a protection fault (out‑of‑bounds error).

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern cloud hypervisors use nested paging to translate guest virtual addresses to host physical memory with minimal overhead. Research on memory compression and tiered memory (DRAM + NVRAM) extends the ideas of paging to new hardware. Look for papers on "buddy system allocator" and "slab allocator" for kernel‑level dynamic memory management. The next topic in the syllabus is the Translation Look‑aside Buffer, which speeds up the page‑table walk.
